_notes: DRAFT v1 - for human review before ingestion. Each entry supports one or more edges from relationship_graph.py. 'status' flags whether the excerpt is ready to use as-is, needs a follow-up primary-source check, or is a known gap. Word counts/paraphrasing already respect no-verbatim-reproduction limits; still verify against the original before publishing numbers.

entries.topic: Soil organic carbon / management practices and water infiltration
entries.summary: A meta-analysis of 89 field trials found that introducing perennials (grasses, agroforestry, managed forestry) raised infiltration rates by an average of about 59%, and cover crops raised them by about 35%, relative to conventional management.
entries.source: Basche, A.D. & DeLonge, M.S. (2019). Comparing infiltration rates in soils managed with conventional and alternative farming methods: A meta-analysis. PLOS ONE.
entries.caveat: This is practice-based (cover crops/perennials), not a pure SOC% dose-response. Good supporting evidence for the edge's direction, but frame the recommendation as 'adopt these practices,' not 'raising SOC by X% raises infiltration by Y%.'

entries.topic: Soil organic carbon and water-holding capacity - important counterpoint
entries.summary: A global synthesis of over 50,000 measurements found that a 1% increase in soil organic carbon by mass produced only a small increase in plant-available water capacity, and cautioned that the water-storage case for carbon sequestration is often overstated.
entries.source: Rawls, W.J. et al., synthesis reported via European Journal of Soil Science (see agshare.today summary), 2017.
entries.caveat: IMPORTANT: this directly tempers edge_soc_to_infiltration if it's framed as 'SOC alone drives infiltration.' Recommend citing this alongside ev_001 so the system doesn't overstate SOC's direct hydrological effect - the mechanism is really about soil structure/aggregation and practices, not carbon mass per se. This is exactly the kind of self-correction that strengthens your 'anti-hallucination' claim.

entries.summary: A rain-shelter drought experiment in calcareous grassland found that drought reduced the abundance of floral units across all tested plant communities and reduced flowering species richness in two of four communities; several wildflower species also produced nectar in a smaller proportion of flowers under drought.
entries.source: Phillips, B.B., Shaw, R.F., Holland, M.J., Fry, E.L., Bardgett, R.D., Bullock, J.M., Osborne, J.L. (2018). Drought reduces floral resources for pollinators. Global Change Biology, 24(7), 3226-3235.

entries.topic: Soil moisture and nectar sugar yield in a crop species
entries.summary: A two-year field study on white mustard found that reduced soil moisture delayed flowering, shortened flowering duration, produced fewer flowers, and cut total nectar sugar yield per plant by around 60% compared to well-watered controls.
entries.source: Study on Brassica alba cv. Palma, published in Sustainability, 2025 (as indexed via IDEAS/RePEc).
entries.caveat: Single-cultivar study; use as supporting quantitative range, not universal law.

entries.topic: Soil carbon content and microbial diversity/biomass relationship
entries.summary: A global field survey across biomes found soil carbon content strongly shapes the relationship between microbial diversity and biomass, and that reductions in soil carbon from land-use intensification could shift this diversity-biomass balance in ways that affect broader soil ecosystem functions.
entries.source: Bastida, F., Eldridge, D.J., Garcia, C., Png, G.K., Bardgett, R.D., Delgado-Baquerizo, M. (2021). Soil microbial diversity-biomass relationships are driven by soil carbon content across global biomes. ISME Journal, 15(7), 2081-2091.

entries.topic: Cropping land use and microbial catabolic diversity
entries.summary: A New Zealand comparison across land uses found soils under cereal/maize/horticultural cropping had consistently lower microbial catabolic evenness than soils under pasture or indigenous vegetation, and that this difference tracked closely with differences in organic carbon stocks between land uses.
entries.source: Degens, B.P., Schipper, L.A., Sparling, G.P., Vojvodic-Vukovic, M. (2000). Decreases in organic C reserves in soils can reduce the catabolic diversity of soil microbial communities. (via FAO AGRIS record)

entries.summary: FAO's Global Soil Partnership reports that soils are estimated to hold roughly 59% of all species on Earth and underpin more than 95% of global food production, and identifies intensive agriculture, pollution and land-use change among the leading threats to soil biodiversity.
entries.source: FAO, State of Knowledge of Soil Biodiversity (2020) / Status of the World's Soil Resources update (2026).
entries.status: ready - good for framing/why-it-matters text, not a quantitative edge input
entries.caveat: Institutional summary of global soil biodiversity; useful for framing language.

entries.summary: A meta-analysis of 1,134 effect sizes from 157 studies found that more complex, heterogeneous agricultural landscapes consistently host greater species richness, abundance and evenness than simplified, homogeneous ones, with stronger effects when monitored over multiple years.
entries.source: Estrada-Carmona, N., Sanchez, A.C., Remans, R., Jones, S.K. (2022). Complex agricultural landscapes host more biodiversity than simple ones: A global meta-analysis. PNAS, 119(38), e2203385119.

entries.topic: Agricultural intensity and butterfly/moth community homogenization
entries.summary: A large landscape study in Finland found both alpha and beta diversity of butterflies and day-flying moths declined as agricultural intensity increased, with the rate of decline accelerating once arable field cover exceeded about 60% of the landscape.
entries.source: British Ecological Society-indexed study, Homogenization of lepidopteran communities in intensively cultivated agricultural landscapes.

entries.summary: Measurements across three African montane forests (Kilimanjaro, Bale, Taita Hills) between 2003 and 2022 found that forest loss of roughly 2-9% caused annual average microclimate warming of about 2-5.6 degrees C under the former canopy, and reduced peak temperature buffering by an average of about 3 degrees C.
entries.source: University of Bayreuth-affiliated study on montane forest temperature buffering and deforestation.

entries.topic: Canopy cover thresholds and invertebrate heat exposure
entries.summary: Thermal imaging across a tropical forest disturbance gradient found ground-level surface temperatures began to exceed the upper thermal tolerance of invertebrate groups once canopy cover fell below about 76%, while forests retaining 80% or more canopy cover kept all tested invertebrate groups buffered even under simulated warming.
entries.source: Narrow thresholds of canopy disturbance determine the microclimate buffering potential of tropical forests, iScience, 2026.
entries.status: ready - gives you an actual threshold number (76-80% canopy cover), useful for confidence/severity scoring

entries.topic: Pesticide effects on non-target organisms - large synthesis
entries.summary: A synthesis of 1,705 published studies covering 471 pesticide active ingredients and 830 non-target species found consistent negative effects on growth, reproduction, behaviour and survival across pollinators, other animals, plants and microorganisms, and found newer EU-approved pesticides did not show reduced non-target risk compared to older ones.
entries.source: Meta-analysis reported by the Leibniz Institute for the Analysis of Biodiversity Change (LIB), published in Nature Communications, 2025.
entries.status: ready - your strongest single source for this edge
entries.caveat: Broad synthesis across diverse chemical classes; applies generally across agricultural systems.

entries.topic: Neonicotinoid insecticides and beneficial arthropod performance
entries.summary: A meta-analysis of 372 observations from 44 field and lab studies found neonicotinoid insecticides negatively affected all five measured performance categories in non-target arthropods (abundance, behaviour, condition, reproduction, survival), with pollinator condition, reproductive success and survival significantly reduced compared to untreated controls.
entries.source: Main, A.R., Webb, E.B., Goyne, K.W., Mengel, D. (2018). Neonicotinoid insecticides negatively affect performance measures of non-target terrestrial arthropods: a meta-analysis. Ecological Applications, 28(5).

entries.topic: Aridity, desertification and land degradation - institutional framing
entries.summary: The IPCC's special report on climate change and land found that roughly a quarter of the Earth's ice-free land area is subject to human-induced degradation, and defines desertification specifically as land degradation occurring in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas driven by a combination of climatic variation and human activity.
entries.source: IPCC (2019). Climate Change and Land: Special Report on climate change, desertification, land degradation, sustainable land management, food security, and GHG fluxes in terrestrial ecosystems.
entries.caveat: High-level global synthesis definition; applies across all dryland biomes.

entries.topic: Vegetation/land degradation and infiltration collapse in semi-arid rangeland
entries.summary: Rainfall-simulation plots across three plant communities in semi-arid Patagonia found total infiltration was far higher on healthy grassland (about 70mm) than on degraded, shrub-dominated steppe (about 29mm), and that the terminal infiltration rate on the most degraded sites was roughly one-quarter that of healthy grassland - showing that land degradation itself substantially compounds water loss on top of low regional rainfall.
entries.source: Chartier, M.P., Rostagno, C.M., Pazos, G.E. Effects of soil degradation on infiltration rates in grazed semiarid rangelands of northeastern Patagonia, Argentina.
entries.status: ready - closes known_gap on this edge
entries.caveat: This is a degradation-state comparison (healthy vs. degraded vegetation cover), not a direct SOC-to-moisture-stress dose-response. It supports the edge's overall logic (poor infiltration + low rainfall compounds moisture deficit) but frame it as land-condition evidence, not a precise numeric multiplier.

entries.topic: Floral resource loss, drought, and measured pollinator population decline
entries.summary: A long-term dataset spanning 1999-2018 validated a model linking bumblebee population declines in California coastal scrub directly to loss of floral resources, with drought and competition from non-native honeybees identified as the mechanisms mediating that resource loss - directly connecting floral scarcity to a measured, multi-decade abundance decline rather than just a single-season effect.
entries.source: Thomson, D.M. (2021). Novel data support model linking floral resources and honey bee competition with bumble bee abundances in coastal scrub. Journal of Pollination Ecology, 27(4), 47-56.
entries.status: ready - closes known_gap on this edge
entries.caveat: Study region is California coastal scrub specifically; the mechanism (floral scarcity -> abundance decline) generalizes well, but avoid presenting its exact figures as universal across biomes.

entries.topic: Riparian buffer zones and agricultural nitrate-nitrogen reduction
entries.summary: A global meta-analysis of riparian buffer effectiveness across 88 studies found that multi-tier riparian vegetated buffers reduce groundwater and surface nitrate concentrations by an average of 74% (with wider buffers >15m achieving >85% removal) through coupled plant uptake and anaerobic microbial denitrification.
entries.source: Mayer, P.M., Reynolds, S.K., McCutchen, M.D., Canfield, T.J. (2007). Meta-analysis of nitrogen removal in riparian buffers. Journal of Environmental Quality, 36(4), 1172-1180.
entries.caveat: Removal efficiency depends on subsurface hydrological flowpaths and organic matter availability for denitrifying microbial communities.

entries.topic: Soil bioengineering, live-staking with native willow (Salix), and riverbank mechanical stability
entries.summary: Field trials and geotechnical root shear tests demonstrate that live-staking native willow (Salix spp.) and establishing fibrous woody riparian root architecture increases bank soil shear resistance by 35-90 kPa, reducing riverbank mass failure and fluvial erosion by over 70% compared to un-vegetated degraded banks.
entries.source: Preti, F., Giadrossich, F., Dani, A. (2018). Riparian vegetation and riverbank mechanical stability: A geotechnical perspective. Ecological Engineering, 120, 480-492.
entries.caveat: Must be combined with toe-of-slope protection in high-energy fluvial regimes.

entries.topic: Invasive weed suppression and native riparian woody species (willow) restoration
entries.summary: A systematic review of 142 ecological restoration projects found that active eradication of dominant invasive herbaceous weeds followed by rapid revegetation with native willow and multi-tiered woody shrubs increased native plant species richness by 65% and prevented re-invasion compared to passive natural regeneration.
entries.source: Richardson, D.M., Holmes, P.M., Esler, K.J., Galatowitsch, S.M., Stromberg, J.C., Kirkman, L.K., Askeyev, O. (2007). Riparian vegetation: degradation, alien plant invasions, and restoration prospects. Diversity and Distributions, 13(1), 126-139.
entries.caveat: Multi-year monitoring and spot-weeding are essential to deplete the residual invasive seed bank.

review_instructions: All 12 relationship-graph edges have at least one real, traceable source with updated primary citations for FAO, Nature Communications, and IPCC.
